newsitem.title: USA: U.S. "concerned" by reported China missile transfer.
newsitem.headline: U.S. "concerned" by reported China missile transfer.

text.p: The United States voiced deep concern on Thursday over reports that China has supplied ballistic missiles to Pakistan but said Washington planned no action at present.

"We are deeply concerned and have been deeply disturbed by many reports we have been seeing about the possible transfer of M-11 missiles to Pakistan," State Department spokesman James Rubin said at a briefing.

Rubin said, however, that the United States had not determined that the transfer of missiles had occurred. "If we do believe the standard of evidence has been met that we have set, which is quite high for a matter like this, we will act according to our laws but, we have not done so."

Rubin was replying to a reporter's question about written comments made by India's junior Foreign Minister Kamala Sinha, who accused China of supplying ballistic missiles to Pakistan and helping its arch-foe build a missile factory.

Both Pakistan and China have denied earlier reports of missile transfers, and Islamabad dismissed fears voiced in the United States and India about its alleged missile development, saying it was doing nothing contrary to its commitments.

India has been reluctant to accuse China directly of supplying ballistic missiles to Pakistan, and Sinha's comments were believed to be the first time India had publicly and unambiguously accused China in this matter.
This latest evidence of conflict in the subcontinent comes as India and Pakistan were gearing up to celebrate the 50th anniversary of their independence from Britain.
At the same time, the United States is taking a new interest in the region, which some have seen as the world's most likely arena for a nuclear conflict.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright has accepted invitations to visit both countries some time this year. She will be the first holder of the office to do so since George Shultz in 1983.

Arms proliferation remains the key U.S. concern on the subcontinent, and led to a diplomatic confrontation in 1996 when the United States and its allies defeated an attempt by India to block a global nuclear test ban treaty.

India and Pakistan are described by Washington as "threshhold" states that could quickly assemble a nuclear weapon if they wished, raising the stakes if they should go to war as they have in the past over the disputed region of Kashmir.
